To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the p53 response in human fibroblasts is triggered by alkali-stable, bulky DNA lesions, not DNA strand breaks; 2) the ATM protein kinase is not required for p53 activation by bulky DNA lesions; and 3) the p53 pathway is activated by persistent DNA lesions, not those removed by excision repair.

the ATM protein is not required for the up-regulation of the tumor suppressor protein p53 following exposure of human fibroblasts with 4-nitoquinoline 1 oxide, a model environmental carcinogenic agent that produces both DNA double-strand breaks and alkali-stabile bulky DNA lesions.

the 4-nitrosquinoline 1 oxide (4NQ0) induced p53 response in diploid fibroblasts is mediated by an ATM-independent, excision repair-dependent mechanism, and that the p33 protein levels are inversely correlated to DNA repair efficiency in fibroblast strains exposed to 4N0Q0, indicating that lesions such as alkali-stable DNA adducts are responsible for triggering the p53 response to this genotoxic agent.

the mechanisms by which cells respond to environmental carcinogens, and in particular, how the DNA repair pathway is linked with cell signalling.
